newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economy not seen suffering much from US-Iraq row.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy not seen suffering much from US-Iraq row.

text.p: Japan's giant economy is seen facing marginal damage from the latest U.S.-Iraq confrontation, which has pushed up global oil prices, economists in Tokyo said on Wednesday.
Any rapid surge in oil prices in theory should worsen Japan's inflationary picture by boosting imported prices, but many doubt if the current oil price surge would last for long.

"In theory, a 10 percent rise in oil prices could push up wholesale prices here by 0.2 point a year, and the impact would become larger if that combined with another rapid yen plunge," said Soichi Okuda, a senior economist at NCB Research Institute.
"But the surge in oil prices has not been that drastic, so its impact on the economy at the moment is limited to being a psychological one," NCB's Okuda said.
Japan is the world's biggest importer of Middle East oil.

On Tuesday, oil prices in New York rallied as high as $24.25 a barrel after the U.S. missile strike against Iraq in response to Baghdad's incursion into Kurdish areas in the north of Iraq. The prices later retreated to close at $23.40 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX).

On Wednesday, the NYMEX crude futures contract, trading in Asia on the after-hours system, rose briefly to $23.65 after a CNN report said the United States had launched a second missile attack against Iraq. But the rally soon petered out.

"If you ask if this is a plus or minus factor (for the economy), it should be minus," said Hiroshi Suzuki, a economist at Norinchukin Research Institute. The U.S-Iraq tension could cut into profits of Japanese oil companies because they may not be able to boost prices of their products fast enough to offset the increased cost of importing oil, he said.
"But I don't think (the Iraq events) alone will spread inflationary concerns here," said Suzuki.
Japan's inflation has been well under control, with consumer prices growing less than 0.5 percent year-on-year and wholesale prices falling from their year-ago levels.

"The Bank of Japan (BOJ), given its role as an inflation watchdog, may feel uneasy about the higher oil prices. But we are not in a situation to see any drastic boost in prices, I think the BOJ will stay calm at the helm," Okuda said.

Expectations for a quick end to the BOJ's current hyper-accommodative credit stance waned after the central bank's key quarterly "tankan" survey, released late last month, disappointed the financial markets as it showed an unexpected decline in companies' business confidence.
On the trade front, some economists said higher oil prices may speed up the tempo in the decline in Japan's contentious current account surplus by boosting the value of imports.
